articles.title: The Internet's Spare Parts Economy: Why Your Network's Most Valuable Asset Might Be the Equipment Sitting on Your Shelf
articles.excerpt: The expensive thing I ever lost was a fifty-dollar part I had never purchased. I did not lose it in a fire or a flood. I lost it in the way many network people lose items: by deciding, calmly and for…
articles.body: The expensive thing I ever lost was a fifty-dollar part I had never purchased. I did not lose it in a fire or a flood. I lost it in the way many network people lose items: by deciding, calmly and for good reasons, that I did not need it yet. The part was a power supply for a switch that had worked perfectly for six years. Nobody thought about it. Then, on a Friday afternoon, it stopped working, and service for a third of an ISP's customers went down. The switch itself was fine. The network design was fine. One tiny component, which a supplier could have sold me for the price of a dinner, turned a quiet Friday into most of a weekend of network downtime. That weekend changed the way I see the shelf in the room. For years I looked at it. Saw clutter, boxes, and money I could not use.

articles.title: SPF passed. DKIM passed. DMARC still failed. Here's why
articles.excerpt: You open the raw headers of an email that landed in spam and see this: Authentication-Results: mx.google.com; dkim=pass header.i=@sendgrid.net header.s=s1; spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=bounces+123@em.sendgr…
articles.body: You open the raw headers of an email that landed in spam and see this: Authentication-Results: mx.google.com; dkim=pass header.i=@sendgrid.net header.s=s1; spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=bounces+123@em.sendgrid.net; dmarc=fail (p=QUARANTINE) header.from=acme.com SPF passed. DKIM passed. DMARC failed. It looks like a bug in Gmail. It isn't. DMARC doesn't ask "did SPF pass?" or "did DKIM pass?". It asks a stricter question: did either of them pass for the same domain your reader sees in the From line? That's called alignment, and it's the most common reason for exactly this result. This post explains alignment in plain terms, shows how to check it with dig and the raw headers, and walks through the five setups that cause it, each with its fix.

articles.title: A Guide to SaaS Signup CNAME Upsert Recovery and Rollback
articles.excerpt: Customer-owned zones preserve control over a customer's mail identity; platform-owned zones give the application a place where it can automate changes directly. TL;DR: commit the tenant reservation an…
articles.body: Customer-owned zones preserve control over a customer's mail identity; platform-owned zones give the application a place where it can automate changes directly. TL;DR: commit the tenant reservation and a durable provisioning intent together, then reconcile DNS outside the signup transaction. Treat CNAME upsert and rollback as recoverable operations, and track SPF, DKIM, and DMARC separately before declaring the mail setup ready. For a hypothetical B2B SaaS signup, I would put cedar.app.example in a platform-owned zone while the customer keeps customer.example and its mail policy. Suppose the CNAME write times out after the signup has committed. My first postmortem question would be: what page fired?

articles.body: Togliere le pause da una registrazione vocale si riduce a quattro numeri: un livello sotto il quale l'audio conta come silenzio, quanto deve durare un tratto silenzioso prima di essere rimosso e quanto margine lasciare su ciascun lato dei pezzi che restano. Il Sound Editor dell'app desktop di osFoundry espone proprio questi quattro valori nella finestra Strip Silence, con i default −48 dB, 50 ms, 5 ms e 20 ms. Qui sotto la stessa operazione viene ricostruita in circa 40 righe di numpy, verificata campione per campione su un file esportato dall'app e poi usata per misurare cosa fa davvero ogni numero. Alla fine, lo stesso lavoro con silenceremove di ffmpeg, che si comporta in modo diverso su un dettaglio facile da non notare.

articles.title: You can see another galaxy with the naked eye — here's how to find it
articles.excerpt: The Andromeda galaxy is one of the most distant things you can see with the naked eye. The difficult part isn't finding it. It's believing that faint smudge really is another galaxy.
articles.body: The first time I showed someone the Andromeda galaxy (M31), our conversation did not go quite as planned. I'd carefully worked my way across the sky, starting from the Great Square of Pegasus and hopping from star to star until I was confident I had the right patch. I pointed the telescope, got M31 in its crosshairs and proudly announced to my wife that I had found the closest giant galaxy to the Milky Way . Would she like to see it? She then stayed quiet for a little too long as she looked through the eyepiece. Then came an unexpected question. "Is it near that little smudge?" Hmmm. "Err, no. It is that little smudge," I replied. There was a pause. Of course, I knew exactly what had happened.

articles.title: Giant exoplanet emerges from the dark when the James Webb Space Telescope turns out the starlight
articles.excerpt: Astronomers have filtered out starlight from James Webb Space Telescope observations to see a giant exoplanet emerge in the darkness.
articles.body: Sometimes science can seem really counter-intuitive. For example, occasionally in astronomy, you can see more with less light. Case in point: the emergence of a giant planet in observations made by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), when astronomers found a way to block out light from the planet's parent star. The extrasolar planet, or exoplanet , in question is 51 Eridani b (51 ERI b), a gas giant with the same mass as around 11 Jupiters that orbits a star located around 97 light-years away. 51 ERI b was discovered back in 2015 by ground-based telescopes, but the planet was missing from observations of the system made by the JWST.

articles.excerpt: The European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has gotten its first close-up look at the Didymos binary asteroid, the first space rock system "punched" by humanity.
articles.body: The Didymos binary asteroid system, as seen by Europe's Hera probe. The main asteroid, Didymos, dominates the frame while just a sliver of its "moonlet," Dimorphos, is visible beneath it. ESA released this image on Nov. 5, 2026. (Image credit: ESA) The European Space Agency 's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has gotten its first close-up look at the Didymos binary asteroid system. If that system sounds familiar, it's because it made headlines in September 2022 when NASA's DART (Double Asteroid Redirection Test) spacecraft smashed into it. The aim of the DART mission was to test whether an impact could divert an asteroid away from a collision course with Earth. The purpose of Hera is to follow up on DART by making up-close observations of the Didymos system.
